note: W1-LIBRARY round 3. The martial skills that are not weapons: sneak, veiling, athletics, acrobatics and security all had zero or near-zero coverage. An Assize investigator concludes there is no order of assassins and prints the appendix that unmakes him; a hunter teaches concealment in a country with no shadows and refuses to write down the fifth lesson; a serjeant-instructor teaches an Imperial column to walk on ground that does not push back and dismisses the alternative in one sentence; a climber writes an advertisement and leaves out the two things he actually does; and a quartermaster writes the province's best manual on opening locks while believing he is writing one on shutting them.

books.title: Report on the Existence, Organisation and Recruitment of the Body Commonly Called the Shadowscales
books.author: compiled for the Provincial Office at Gideon by an officer of the Assize whose name has been removed from every surviving copy
books.unreliability: An investigator who is careful, methodical, honest about his sources and comprehensively played. Every witness he found was a witness somebody was willing for him to find. He suspects this in one paragraph near the end and does not follow it, because following it would mean the report cannot be written, and he had been given a year.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Concludes on the balance of the evidence that the body does not exist as an organisation and that the name covers an assortment of local practices. His own appendix contains four separate accounts, from four regions, of the same recruitment rite described in the same order.
books.text:
This report was commissioned after the matter at the Lilmoth customs house and has taken 14 months. I have gone where I was permitted to go and have spoken to whoever would speak to me, and I have set out below what I found, what I could not find, and what I believe, in that order and clearly separated, because I have read enough Office reports where those three were mixed to know what it costs.

I. THE CLAIM AS IT IS USUALLY MADE.

The claim runs as follows. Argonian hatchlings born under a particular alignment of the moons are given up at birth by custom, without argument, to an order of assassins. They are trained from the egg. They serve the Dark Brotherhood, or the King of Argonia, or the Hist, depending on who is telling it. They are the reason no Imperial column goes 2 days inland.

Every Imperial in this province believes some version of this and almost none of them can say where they first heard it.

II. WHAT I HAVE ESTABLISHED.

*The custom of giving up.* Real, and I have documentary confirmation. Six birth registers from the coastal settlements, kept for the Office's own census, record hatchlings entered and then struck through with a note in the margin. The notes vary: *given*, *to the moons*, *not counted*, and at Soulrest simply a hooked mark that the clerk there told me means the same. The count over 30 years, in the 6 settlements I have registers for, is 41.

*The birth-timing.* Also real, so far as a register can show it. Of the 41, I have dates for 33, and 29 of the 33 fall within 3 days of the same conjunction. That is not a coincidence and I do not offer it as one.

*The training.* Here the evidence stops dead.

I have no witness who has seen it. I have no location. I have no name of an instructor, no supply return, no dispute over a payment, no complaint from a neighbour, nothing. In 14 months of asking, in 8 settlements, I have not found one person who will say they know where a given child went.

III. WHAT THE PROVINCE SAYS, AND HOW IT SAYS IT.

I want to record the *manner* of the answers, because it is the most informative thing in this report.

When I asked about the Dres slavers, people were angry and told me a great deal.

When I asked about the Ford, people were pleased and told me a great deal, some of it untrue.

When I asked about the under-moon births, people were *helpful*. Uniformly. Politely. At length. And every single account I was given was the same account, in the same order, with the same 3 details, from Archon to Soulrest, in households that have no correspondence with each other and in 2 cases could not have.

The 3 details are these. The child is taken at night by somebody who is not from the settlement. The mother is given a token — described variously as a stone, a shell, a knot of cord — and keeps it. And nobody in the settlement asks, ever, and the not-asking is described as a kindness to the mother rather than as a rule.

I have put 4 of these accounts in the appendix in full and the reader may compare them.

IV. THE INCIDENTS.

The Office's file holds 9 deaths over 40 years attributed in official correspondence to this body. I have examined each.

Four are plainly other things. A factor at Archon whose death the surgeon recorded as apoplexy. A serjeant at Thorn killed in a brawl with 3 witnesses. Two drownings.

Three are unexplained and I am not going to pretend otherwise. A Dres agent at Blackrose, in a locked upper room, in 3E 411. A clerk of the Assize at Lilmoth, in 3E 418, in a corridor with 2 guards at one end and a wall at the other. And the matter at the customs house last year, which is the reason for this report and which I am not permitted to describe.

Two I cannot classify. Both were men who died of nothing at all, in their beds, in good health, in the same month, having both been involved in the same lease.

V. WHAT I BELIEVE, AND HERE I AM GIVING AN OPINION.

I do not believe there is an order.

I believe there is a *custom* of giving up under-moon hatchlings, which is old and real and universal on this coast. I believe the children go somewhere. And I believe that where they go is 41 different places over 30 years — to relatives, to keepers, to the deep settlements, to whoever in a given season is willing — and that the province has wrapped a single terrible story around 41 quiet private arrangements, and finds the story useful.

Useful how. Consider what the story buys them. Every Imperial official in this province, from the Prefect down, conducts himself on the assumption that there are people he cannot see who will kill him if he goes too far. Not one of us can say where the assumption came from. And there has been no column inland in 36 years.

A province that cannot field an army has manufactured a deterrent out of a birth custom and a small number of unexplained deaths, and it has done it so patiently and so consistently that its own people may believe it. That is my conclusion and I am aware it will not be popular.

VI. AGAINST MYSELF.

Three things I cannot answer, which I set down so that whoever reads this after me does not have to find them the hard way.

The 3 unexplained deaths are unexplained. My reading requires them to be coincidence or ordinary murder, and a locked upper room at Blackrose is not ordinary.

The uniformity of the accounts is not what an assortment of private arrangements produces. Forty-one families improvising 41 solutions do not converge on a stone, a night, and a stranger. I have written above that I found the manner of the answers informative and I have not let myself finish the thought.

And the last one, which I would rather not put in an official report and am putting in.

In 14 months, everybody I asked, answered. Nobody refused me. Nobody was frightened of me. Nobody was frightened of *them*, in a province where a mother giving up a child at night to a stranger is described to a Legion officer as a kindness.

Either there is nothing to be frightened of, which is my conclusion.

Or I was shown a road and walked down it for 14 months and wrote what I was given at the end of it.

I have no way to distinguish those two, and I want the Office to know that I know it.

*(Appendix A, containing the four accounts, is missing from every copy the Office holds. Appendix B, the birth registers, is intact.)*

VII. THE OFFICE'S EARLIER ATTEMPTS, WHICH I FOUND LATE AND WHICH I WISH I HAD FOUND FIRST.

In my eleventh month I was given the run of a press in the Gideon registry that nobody had opened since it was filled.

This is not the first report on this subject. It is the fourth.

*3E 361.* A memorandum of 9 pages by a Prefect whose name is legible. He concludes that the body exists, is organised out of Helstrom, and has perhaps 40 members. His evidence is 3 informants, all paid, none named, and a map with a circle on it.

*3E 388.* A report of 30 pages by an officer of the Assize. He concludes that the body does not exist and that the name covers an assortment of local practices, and his reasoning is very nearly mine, arrived at from different settlements, 40 years earlier.

*3E 404.* A single sheet. It says that the matter has been enquired into twice and that a third enquiry is not recommended, and it is signed by somebody senior enough that no name was thought necessary.

*3E 425.* Mine.

I want the reader to sit with the shape of that. Every 25 years or so this Office sends somebody out for a year. The somebody comes back with a conclusion. The conclusion alternates.

VIII. WHAT THE ALTERNATION MEANS, AND I HAVE TWO READINGS.

*The first reading, which is the comfortable one.* There is nothing there, the evidence is thin, and a thin evidence base supports whichever conclusion the investigator's temperament prefers. A credulous man finds an order. A sceptical man finds a custom. Both write 30 pages.

*The second reading.* Something is being managed. An enquiry that concludes there is nothing is an enquiry that ends. An enquiry that concludes there is something is an enquiry that gets a successor, and a successor is another year of an Imperial officer walking around the settlements asking questions. On the second reading the alternation is not a defect of the evidence. It is a rhythm, and the rhythm keeps the Office looking at this subject at a comfortable interval and never at an uncomfortable one.

I cannot choose between these and I am not going to pretend to.

IX. THE INTERVIEWS I HAVE NOT REPORTED ABOVE.

Three, and I kept them out of the body of the report because none of them is evidence and all 3 have stayed with me.

*A rootkeeper at Helstrom, month 4.* I asked whether the under-moon children were given to the Hist. She said the question could not be put in her language and that she would answer the question I had meant to ask instead, which was whether they were given to anybody. She said: they are given up. She would not go further and she was not being evasive; she was being precise, and I did not understand the distinction then and I do not now.

*A woman at Soulrest, month 7, who had given up a child 19 years earlier.* She showed me the token. It is a shell, drilled, on a cord. I asked whether she had ever seen the child again and she said no. I asked whether she would want to and she thought about it for a long time and said that she had decided a long time ago that the answer was no, and that deciding it had taken 9 years, and that she had been given the decision to make and she counted that a kindness.

I asked who had given her the decision to make. She said: the same one who took him.

*A serjeant of the Ninth, month 12, who had served 30 years.* Not a witness to anything. I asked him, as I asked everybody by then, whether he believed in them.

He said: I've never seen one and I've never met anyone who has.

Then he said: I've also never in 30 years gone more than 2 days inland, and neither has anybody I've served with, and no officer has ever ordered me not to.

X. RECOMMENDATION.

That no further enquiry be made for 25 years, at which point somebody will make one.

I put that down as a joke and then I read it back and I have decided to leave it in the report.

books.title: Not Being Seen in a Country That Has No Shadows: For Hunters, and For Whoever Else Is Reading This
books.author: Uxith-Ei, hunter, at the Thornmarsh edge, who has taught this to 30 young ones and writes it down because she is getting old
books.unreliability: A teaching book with a hole in it exactly where the interesting part would be. Her fifth lesson describes something she calls the quiet and she declines to say what it is or how it is done, twice, and then uses it as a premise in the sixth lesson.
books.text:
Everything the Imperials write about not being seen is about shadows. Stand in a shadow. Move between shadows. Wait for the dark.

There are no shadows here worth the name. The light comes down through 40 feet of leaf and comes up off the water and comes sideways off every wet surface in the province, and by the time it reaches you it has been everywhere and it comes from everywhere and it does not make shadows, it makes a green fog with things in it.

So this is a different craft and I am writing it because the young ones I taught it to are teaching it wrong.

THE FIRST LESSON. YOU ARE NOT HIDING FROM EYES.

An eye in this country is nearly useless past 30 paces and everything living here knows it.

You are hiding from the water, from the reeds, from the birds, and from the smell of yourself, and of those four the birds are the one that will finish you.

A young one who has learned to keep still and been praised for it will lie in a reed bed being perfectly still while every heron for a mile stands up and looks at where she is, and she will not understand why the deer went, because she was still, because she did what she was taught.

THE SECOND LESSON. THE WATER TELLS.

Still water carries a mark from a leg for a long time. Not a ripple. A ripple is nothing, a ripple dies. What carries is the film — the skin on the top of still water with the dust on it — and a leg going through it opens a line in the dust that stays open, and anything downstream of you can read it like a road.

So: move in moving water when you can, and when you cannot, move slowly enough that the film closes behind you before it opens in front of you. It is slower than anybody wants. Half a pace to a breath. A young one who is impatient will do 40 paces in the time I do 10 and will arrive at nothing.

And never cross a still channel at right angles. Go along it. A line down the length of a channel could be a fish or a snake or a stick. A line across it is a person and everything in the marsh knows it.

THE THIRD LESSON. REEDS ARE NOT A WALL.

The young ones think a reed bed is cover. It is not cover. It is a crowd, and you are in it, and a crowd shows a person moving through it because the crowd moves.

Reeds move together. Wind takes the whole bed and lays it one way and it comes back one way. A person going through lays a line of them the other way and stands them up again 3 at a time, and to anything watching the bed from outside it is as clear as a hand going through hair.

The way through a reed bed is with the wind and not across it, and in the moment the wind is already moving them, and in short goes with long waits. When the bed is still you are still. When the bed goes over, you go 4 paces.

I have watched an Imperial scout cross a bed at Thornmarsh in a dead calm, very slowly, very carefully, doing everything he had been taught, and there was a line of standing-up reeds behind him a child could have followed.

THE FOURTH LESSON. THE SMELL.

Nobody wants to hear this one.

You smell. You smell of smoke and of oil on your weapon and of what you ate and of the settlement you slept in, and in wet air a smell does not go up and away as it does in dry country. It lies down and it goes with the water.

So: downwind is not enough. Down-*water*. Find which way the surface is going and be on the wrong end of it, and if the water and the wind disagree, believe the water.

Wash in the channel you are hunting, without soap, the night before. Leave the oiled weapon behind if you can bear to and take the one that is only wood and stone. Do not eat the smoked fish. I have said that last one to 30 young ones and 30 young ones have eaten the smoked fish.

THE FIFTH LESSON, WHICH I WILL NOT WRITE DOWN PROPERLY.

There is a thing the old hunters do that the young ones call the quiet.

It is not a trick of the body and it is not a spell in the way your keepers do spells and I am not going to describe it in a book that a factor at Gideon might buy for 3 drakes.

I will say what it does, because that much is fair. In the quiet, a thing that is looking for you looks at you and does not find you there. Not because you are hidden. You are standing in the open. It looks at the place you are and its attention goes past.

I will also say what it costs, because a young one should know before they ask. It cannot be held for long. It cannot be held at all if you are frightened, which is when you want it. And it does not work twice on the same creature in the same day, and nobody has ever been able to tell me why.

Ask a hunter. Ask in person, and ask more than once, and expect to be refused the first time.

THE SIXTH LESSON. WHAT ALL OF THIS IS FOR.

Here I will disagree with everybody who has taught this before me, including the person who taught me.

Not being seen is not a way of getting close. It is a way of *choosing*.

The young ones all want to learn this so they can creep up on something. Fine, and it works, and a deer taken from 6 paces is a deer taken. But the real use of it, the one you will still be using when your hands have gone, is that a person who cannot be found gets to decide whether there is a hunt at all.

You will meet things in this marsh that you cannot beat. You will meet people you cannot beat. And the whole of what I have written here comes down to the fact that on the day you meet them, you will be the only one of the two of you who knows the meeting is happening.

That is worth more than any weapon anyone in this province has ever carried, and it is why I have taught it to 30 young ones and refused it to 4.

THE LAST THING, AND IT IS NOT A LESSON.

They will tell you at Gideon that we are all born knowing this. It is said kindly and it is meant as a compliment and it makes me tired.

I was 9 years learning it. My teacher was 11 years learning it and was better than me. The young ones I taught who came from the towns took longer and 2 of them are the best I ever taught.

Nobody is born knowing anything. Some of us were born somewhere that made us practise.

THE SEVENTH LESSON. THE NIGHT, WHICH IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK.

The Imperials wait for dark. Do not wait for dark.

At night the marsh is loud and everything in it is awake and listening, and the things that hunt at night are hunting with something better than eyes. In the dark you cannot see where you are putting your feet, so you put them badly, so the water tells on you, and the whole of the second lesson goes to nothing.

The hour to move is the hour before the light comes properly, when the mist is on the water and has not lifted. The mist is a wall as good as any dark and it does not stop you seeing your own feet, and the things that hunt at night have gone down and the things that hunt by day have not come up.

If you must move in the dark, move in water and not on land, and go slower than you think is silly.

THE EIGHTH LESSON. WHAT WATCHES.

Learn the birds before you learn anything else in this book. I have put it last and I should have put it first and I am too old to write it again.

*Herons.* The worst. They stand up and they look and they do not go, and a standing heron looking at a reed bed has told everything with 4 legs in a mile where you are. Never approach a heron. Go round the whole reach it is standing in.

*The small brown ones in the reeds.* They go up in a burst. That burst is a shout and it can be heard from a great way off, and it is the sound every hunter in the province listens for when they are the one waiting.

*Crows on a drying rack.* They do not care about you and they will not move and they are the best cover in the province, because anything watching a settlement watches the crows, and crows that have not moved mean nothing has happened.

*The things in the water that are not birds.* If the small fish go out of a channel ahead of you, something is in it. It may be you. It may not be you. Wait and find out from where you are.

THE NINTH LESSON. GOING BACK.

Everybody teaches going in. Nobody teaches going back and going back is where people are caught.

You are tired. You are carrying something. You are pleased with yourself, and being pleased with yourself is a state in which a person makes noise.

And you know the way, and knowing the way is the trap, because you will take the same line back that you took in, and the line you took in is written on the water and on the reeds behind you for anything that came along afterwards and read it.

Never go back the way you came. Never. Go along, not back, and come home by another channel even if it costs you the rest of the day.

I have said this to 30 young ones. I have broken it twice myself, both times carrying something heavy, both times within a mile of home, and the second time is the reason I no longer hunt alone.

THE TENTH LESSON, WHICH IS FOR THE ONES WHO ARE NOT HUNTING.

I know who else reads this kind of book.

I will not help you and I will not refuse to. Everything above is about deer and about the things that eat deer and it happens to be about people, and I cannot write it one way and not the other, and I have thought about that for a year and decided to write it anyway.

But I will put one thing at the end, for whoever you are.

Everything in this book makes you harder to find. Nothing in it makes you harder to *live with*. A person who has learned all of this and used it on their neighbours is a person their settlement will one day decide about, quietly, without telling them it is deciding, and the deciding will go the way it goes, and there is no lesson in here that helps at that point.

Take it hunting.

books.title: How a Man Gets Anywhere Here Carrying Anything, Set Down for the Cohort's Recruits and Nobody Else
books.author: Serjeant-Instructor Peris Vulso, Ninth Cohort, depot at Thorn
books.unreliability: Practical, tested and correct within its limits, and its limits are the ones the Legion has chosen. Everything in it is about how to march an Imperial soldier across a marsh in Imperial kit, and the alternative — carrying less — is dismissed in one sentence as a discipline problem.
books.text:
Recruits arrive believing that walking is a thing they already know how to do. This lasts about 3 miles.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT ABOUT WALKING HERE.

On a road, your leg swings forward and your foot lands and the ground pushes back at you. All of the work is done by the ground, for nothing.

In this province the ground does not push back. It gives. Then it gives a bit more. Then it holds your foot, and you have to take it out again. Taking a foot out of marsh mud costs about as much as putting it in.

So every step is two steps' work. The second one is done by the hip and the belly. Recruits have no muscle there at all, because roads have never asked them for any.

That is why a fit man off a boat from Anvil is finished in an afternoon. And why a small woman from the weirs who looks like nothing at all is still going at dusk. It is not spirit. She has different muscles. She grew up on different ground.

THE STEP.

Short. Flat. Landing under you, not out in front.

A long stride puts your foot down ahead of your weight. Then your weight arrives. Then the foot goes in. Now you must lift a leg that has a body leaning over it.

A short stride puts the foot under the weight from the beginning. The foot goes in less deep. The lift is straight up.

Flat means the whole sole at once. Heel first is for roads. Heel first here drives the heel in and levers the toe up, and you will pull your own boot off within a mile.

Lift the whole leg with the hip. Do not pull with the ankle. Recruits who pull with the ankle get the marsh cramp in the shin on the second day. It is very painful. It goes away in a week. There is no cure but doing it right.

THE FOOT COMING OUT.

Straight up. Straight. Angle it and the suction takes the boot.

Count how many boots the depot has replaced this season. It is 31. Every one was pulled off by a man twisting his foot out of mud because he was in a hurry.

THE POLE.

Every man carries one. Not for the boat. For walking.

A pole taken in both hands, planted a pace ahead and slightly to the side, gives you a third leg on ground you have not tested. Across a day it takes about a fifth of the work off your legs. A fifth is the difference between arriving able to fight, and arriving.

Plant. Weight on it. Step past it. Pull it out. It is a rhythm. After a week you will do it asleep.

The auxiliaries pole all day without appearing to move their arms. It takes 2 years to look like that.

The pole is also how you find out what you are about to stand on. That has saved more men in this cohort than any weapon in the stores.

CARRYING.

Weight high and close. On the back, up between the shoulders, strapped so it does not swing.

A pack that sits low and swings will take you over sideways on ground that has already got your foot. A man on his side in a marsh with a full pack cannot always get up without help. Every serjeant in this province has stood over a recruit explaining that to him while he lies there.

Shield on the back, not on the arm, until the last mile. Sword on the belt and short. Bill carried across the shoulders in both hands, which is also a rest for the arms.

Water on the front. Always on the front. You want to reach it without stopping. A column that has to halt to drink halts 20 times.

THE PACE, AND THE ARGUMENT ABOUT IT.

Twelve miles is a day. The instruction says so. The instruction is right. Every new officer wants to prove otherwise.

Rest on the hour, standing, on the pole, for the count of 100. Not sitting. A man who sits in wet kit stiffens. A column that has sat down takes 10 minutes to be a column again.

I have been asked why we do not simply carry less, as the auxiliaries do. They go twice as far and arrive fresh. They carry a spear, a knife, a bag and nothing else.

The answer is that a soldier is his kit. A cohort that has left its kit behind to go faster is a mob that has arrived early. This has been settled by better men than me and I will not have it argued in my depot.

WATER, WHICH KILLS MORE RECRUITS THAN ANYTHING.

You will not feel thirsty. That is the whole trap.

In a dry country you feel thirst because you can feel yourself drying. Here the air is wet and your skin is wet and you are sweating into a shirt that never dries. You will lose 3 quarts in a morning and never once feel dry.

So drink on the hour whether you want to or not. Every hour. Fill at every clean channel. Let the serjeant tell you which are clean. If you are not sure, do not.

The second week of every intake there is a man who goes down at the ninth mile with his eyes rolling and his skin dry. The men around him say he must have taken a fever. It is never a fever. He did not drink.

I have lost 4 in 9 years. Every one of them was a strong man who was proud of not stopping.

SWIMMING, BRIEFLY.

You will be told the auxiliaries do not drown. They do not. You will.

Nobody in this cohort swims in armour. Nobody swims a channel he has not been told is safe by somebody local. If a channel must be crossed and there is no crossing, that is what rope and poles are for. The drill is in the depot book.

I would rather spend 2 hours on a rope than write another letter to Cyrodiil.

books.title: Getting Up a Stone Nest, and Getting Down Again, Which Is the Difficult Half
books.author: Aneesh-Doon, who fetches things off the terraces at Ixt-Shaneekh for antiquarians and charges by the height
books.unreliability: He has a business and this is partly an advertisement, and he is careful to leave out the two things he actually does that nobody else has worked out. He says so. He also names a price list halfway through and then a different one at the end.
books.text:
I fetch things off the terraces. Antiquarians point at something and I go and get it and they pay me, and they always pay me less than they said because they always say the thing was smaller than they thought.

I have been asked by 3 different Imperials to explain how it is done, and I have decided to write it because 2 of them have now tried it themselves and one of them is dead.

THE THING NOBODY BELIEVES UNTIL THE SECOND TERRACE.

The stone is not the danger. The stone is 3,000 years old and it has been holding itself up for all of it and it will hold you.

The danger is what has grown on it. Every face of every terrace at Ixt-Shaneekh is under a skin of wet moss, weed, and a black slime that comes off in sheets. You will put a hand on a ledge that is sound and the ledge will be sound and the thing on top of the ledge will slide, with your hand on it, and you will go.

So the first work of a climber here is cleaning, not climbing. I go up with a scraper and I clear every hold I am going to use before I use it, and I do it on the way up, and it doubles the time and it is the whole of why I am alive.

An Imperial will not do this. I have watched them. They see a hold, they test it by pushing on it, it does not move, and they trust it. Pushing tells you the stone is sound. It does not tell you the moss is.

Test by *pulling sideways*. Always sideways. A slime layer holds against a push and goes against a shear.

THE ROUTE.

Never straight up a face.

The terraces are steps and the steps have corners, and a corner gives you two surfaces at once, and two surfaces is the difference between hanging on and standing. Go up the corners, even where it is 3 times as far.

Look for the drains. Every terrace at every stone nest I have been on has channels cut into it for water, and a drain channel is a groove as wide as a leg with two walls, and you can put your back on one wall and your feet on the other and go up it like walking. The old people cut them for water and they are the best ladders in the province and nobody has ever thanked them for it.

Avoid the carved faces. It looks like there are holds all over a carved face. There are, and every one of them was cut by somebody who did not expect a person to hang from it, and the carving is shallower than it looks and it is the first thing on a terrace to go soft.

GOING DOWN, WHICH IS THE PART THAT KILLS PEOPLE.

Everyone thinks about getting up. Getting up is ambition and ambition carries you.

Coming down you are tired, you are carrying something you were paid to carry, and you cannot see your feet. The hold you are reaching for with a foot is somewhere under you and you have to find it blind, and if you cannot find it you have to come back up, and coming back up when your arms have gone is how people fall.

Rules for coming down, and I have never broken one:

Come down the way you went up. Not a shorter way. Not the way that looks easier from above. Everything looks easier from above.

Come down before you are tired, which means turning round at half your strength and not at all of it. The antiquarian standing at the bottom will tell you it is only another 2 terraces. He is at the bottom.

Never come down carrying a thing in your hand. Bag it, sling it, drop it on a line if it will survive the drop, and if it will not survive the drop it will not survive you.

And test every hold again on the way down even though you used it on the way up. You cleaned it going up and then you stood on it, and standing on wet moss makes it into wet slime.

THE DROP.

Sometimes you will come off. I have come off 4 times in 19 years.

Twice I landed on the terrace below, which is what the terraces are for from a climber's point of view — they are steps and a step is never more than a body's length and a half.

The trick, if it is a trick, is to go down the face and not out from it. A person who pushes off in a panic goes out into the air and clears the terrace below and then it is 6 terraces and not 1. Stay in. Scrape all the way down if you must. Skin grows.

Land loose and roll backwards up the slope and not forwards down it.

WHAT I AM NOT PUTTING IN THIS BOOK.

There are 2 things I do that nobody else who does this does, and I am not writing them down, because this is how I feed my household.

One of them is about the drains and the other is about the wet season, and if an antiquarian wants to know either one they may hire me, at 15 drakes the terrace, which is the honest rate.

WHAT I CHARGE.

Fifteen drakes the terrace up to the fourth, 25 above it, and 40 for anything on the top platform at Ixt-Shaneekh, and I will not go on the top platform after the third hour of the afternoon and I will not explain why, and I have lost 2 commissions over it and I would lose them again.

I have raised these prices since the first part of this book was written and I am not going back to change them.

books.title: Of Locks, Bars, and the Opening of Armouries: A Manual for Quartermasters, With a Chapter That Should Not Be In It
books.author: Quartermaster-Clerk Ilvo Sarn, stores at Gideon, 4th issue, and the Office has requested the 5th omit chapter 6
books.unreliability: A completely competent manual for keeping things locked, whose sixth chapter explains at length how each of its own recommendations is defeated. He believes he is arguing for better locks. He has written the best instruction in the province on opening them and it is in print at every station.
books.text:
Fourth issue. Every quartermaster in the province is to hold a copy. Every quartermaster is to be able to produce it.

1. WHAT AN ARMOURY IS FOR.

It is not for keeping weapons safe. Weapons are not in danger.

It is for keeping the count honest. Every rule in this book exists so that a man may open a door, count 40 spears, write 40 in a book, and be believed by somebody in Cyrodiil a year later.

A quartermaster who has understood that will run a good store with 3 bad locks. One who has not will run a bad store with 9 good ones.

2. THE THREE FASTENINGS THIS OFFICE ISSUES.

*The staple and bar.* An iron bar dropped into two staples across a door, with a pin through the bar. Cheap. Strong. It cannot be picked, because there is nothing to pick.

*The warded lock.* A key with cuts in it. The cuts must pass a set of fixed obstructions inside the lock before the bolt will turn. Issued for all interior doors and for chests.

*The Imperial double.* Two wards. Two bolts. Two keys, held by two people. Neither turns alone. Issued for the powder store and for nothing else. I have applied 3 times for one on the main door at Gideon. I have been refused 3 times, on grounds of cost.

3. THE KEYS.

The whole of security in this province is the keys. None of it is the locks.

Keys are held on the person, on a cord, day and night. Not on a hook. Not in a drawer. Not, as I found at one station I will not name, hung on a nail beside the door they open, on the inside, where a hand through a shutter reaches them.

Keys are not lent. A quartermaster who cannot be present unlocks the door himself, or the door stays shut. If that means a serjeant waits an hour, the serjeant waits an hour. He may complain to me.

Every key in this province is listed by number in the station book, with the name of the person holding it. The list is read out at every quarterly muster. Aloud. By name.

4. THE COUNT.

Weekly, by the quartermaster, alone. Monthly, by the quartermaster and one officer, together. Quarterly, against the book, with the book read out.

Count what is there. Do not count what should be there.

I have had two clerks in 9 years who counted the book and then looked at the shelf to confirm it. Both were honest men. Both of their stores were short.

5. THE DAMP, WHICH IS THE REAL ENEMY.

Every lock in this province rusts.

A warded lock left 3 months without oil in the wet season will not turn. The response of every serjeant in the Empire to a lock that will not turn is to force it. A forced lock is a broken lock. A broken lock is an open store.

Oil every lock monthly. Wax the key. Work every lock in the station once a week, whether it needs opening or not.

More stores have been lost in this province to rust than to theft. The margin would embarrass me to write down.

6. HOW EACH OF THE ABOVE IS DEFEATED.

The Office has instructed me to remove this chapter from the next issue.

I have written it anyway. In 9 years I have recovered 6 stores that were opened. In every case the method was one of the following. In every case the quartermaster told me afterwards that he had not known it could be done.

A man cannot guard against a thing he has not been told about. I would rather this chapter were read by 400 quartermasters and 3 thieves than by 3 thieves alone.

*The staple and bar.* The bar cannot be picked. The staple can be prised. It is set into wood. Wood in this climate is soft within 2 years of being set. A lever behind the staple takes the whole fitting out of the frame in less time than it takes to describe. **Remedy:** set staples through the frame with a plate on the far side, not into it. Inspect the wood, not the iron.

*The warded lock.* A ward is an obstruction. The right key passes it. The wrong key does not. Now take an ordinary key and file away everything except the part that turns the bolt. It passes every ward there is, because there is nothing left of it to obstruct. Such a key is made in an evening. It opens every warded lock of the same pattern in the province. The Office buys its locks in one pattern, by the crate. **Remedy:** none that this Office will pay for. The ward is an old idea and it was overtaken a long time ago. If the store matters, use a bar.

*The Imperial double.* Sound. Both of the failures I have seen were the two key-holders agreeing. No lock addresses that.

*The hinge.* Every lock in this book secures the opening edge of a door. No lock in this book secures the hanging edge. Drive the pins out and the door comes off the other way, entire. The lock is still locked. The quartermaster finds it locked and reports nothing wrong. **Remedy:** peen the pins over. It takes a hammer and 4 minutes. I have not found a station in this province where it has been done.

*The wall.* Twice out of the 6, they did not use the door.

7. CONCLUSION.

A lock is a way of finding out that somebody wanted in badly enough to leave a mark. That is all any of them do.

Keep the count honest. Keep the keys on your body. Oil the iron. Peen your pins. Write down what you actually saw.

The rest of this is ironmongery.
